summary: EARTHSCAN is a NASA data trend-investigation project with two components: a scientific analysis and an educational detective game. We chose total column ozone as the variable, and made a daily series of 3,660 values from early 2016 to early 2026 and looked for a trend in it. Significance was then tested using linear regression (slope 0.00131 DU/day, p = 0.0042) and the Mann-Kendall test (Z = 2.939, p = 0.0033). Both show a small but significant increase of about 0.48 DU per year. Data quality and limitations including autocorrelation, seasonality, and short record were also discussed. We show how Giovanni, AppEEARS, Hydrology Time Series, NOAA CDO, KNMI, SWOT and RADARSAT extend this same method to water, ice and land. This matters because ozone shields life from harmful UV, and separating real trends from noise is a core Earth-science skill. The detective game teaches that skill to learners, and it links the result to ozone-layer recovery under the Montreal Protocol.
details:
EARTHSCAN investigates whether a NASA Earth-science variable shows a real trend. We chose total column ozone, selected a study region and a ten-year window (early 2016 to early 2026), and built a daily time series of 3,660 values. We plotted it and fitted a linear trend. We then tested significance with two methods: linear regression (slope 0.00131 DU/day, p = 0.0042) and the non-parametric Mann–Kendall test (Z = 2.939, p = 0.0033). Both show a small but significant rise of about 0.48 DU per year. The project also includes a detective game of five cases on spotting trends, separating noise and seasonality from real change, understanding p-values, and reaching a final verdict.

Benefits and intended impact

The project shows a clear, repeatable way to tell a real environmental trend from noise. It reports effect size and limitations, not just a p-value. The game turns these ideas into an activity for students and the public. Our aim is to build trend literacy and to connect the result to ozone-layer recovery under the Montreal Protocol.

Tools and technologies

  • NASA time-series data and tools, including Giovanni
  • Python for the statistical analysis and the time-series graph
  • PowerPoint for the final presentation and game

We also planned cross-checks and extensions with AppEEARS, Hydrology Time Series, NOAA Climate Data Online, KNMI Climate Explorer, SWOT, and RADARSAT Constellation data.

Creativity

We framed the analysis as a “trend detective” investigation and paired it with a game, so the project both analyses data and teaches how to read it.

Factors we considered

We checked data completeness and noted autocorrelation, the strong seasonal cycle, and the short ten-year record. We also warned that annual and daily rates are only comparable for complete years. We kept our claims modest: the rise fits ozone recovery but does not prove its cause.
